questions.q: If you stretch a rubber band, is it still a rubber band?
questions.a: Yes, it is still a rubber band. A wrong answer suggests the student confuses "shape change" with "substance change," failing to realize the material identity remains constant.

questions.q: When you dissolve salt in water, does the salt disappear and become a new substance, or does it stay as salt?
questions.a: The salt stays as salt, it just changes its state (by mixing/dissolving). A wrong answer reveals the misconception that if you cannot see the solid particles, they must have vanished or changed into something else.

questions.q: You have a metal wire. You bend it into a circle. Has a new substance been formed?
questions.a: No. Step 1: Identify the material (metal wire). Step 2: Observe the change (bending). Step 3: Check if the material identity changed (it is still metal). Step 4: Conclude it is a physical change. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks physical manipulation equals a chemical creation.

questions.q: Compare tearing a piece of paper to cutting a piece of wood. How are they similar in terms of physical change?
questions.a: Both involve changing the size and shape of the original material without creating a new substance. A wrong answer indicates difficulty in generalizing the concept of "physical change" across different types of materials.

questions.q: If a boy breaks a glass bottle, is this a physical change? Justify your answer.
questions.a: Yes, it is a physical change because the glass shards are still glass. The substance has not changed its identity; only its size and shape have changed. A wrong answer implies the student equates "destruction" or "damage" with "chemical change."

questions.q: Think of a real-world object in your kitchen. Describe how you could perform a physical change on it.
questions.a: An example would be crushing a dry biscuit into crumbs. The answer is valid if the student identifies that while the biscuit looks different, it is still the same material. A poor answer would suggest something like "burning a match," which is a chemical change.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: A physical change is a change in the form, shape, size, or state of a ______ where no new material is created.
Fill in the blank: If you crumple it into a ball or tear it into tiny confetti ______, has the paper suddenly turned into wood or plastic?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to classify various common changes as "physical" by demonstrating that the substance remains unchanged in its identity.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: If you crumple it into a ball or tear it into tiny ______ pieces, has the paper suddenly turned into wood or plastic?
